source.title_on_document: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Human Creativity Through Real-Time Evaluative Feedback

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials, PDF pp. 39-52; supporting text on pp. 40-42 and Tables S1-S9 on pp. 43-51. Materials, data, and scripts are also linked at https://osf.io/6k52d/?view_only=398df4fd924440ee9387af4f6434d422 (PDF pp. 2, 15).
supplement.holds: Model-training and validation details; invalid-response screening; analyzed-sample demographics (Table S1); participant-level self-rating/originality correlations (Tables S2 and S5); full originality mixed-model coefficients and standard errors (Tables S3 and S6); mediation coefficients and confidence intervals (Tables S4 and S7); and alternative evaluation-accuracy analyses (Tables S8 and S9). The full model coefficient tables are included in this PDF. Cluster-robust sensitivity estimates are described as unreported (PDF p. 18, Analysis strategy).

paper_design_summary: Study 1 analyzed 554 adults recruited online who generated design solutions with continuous GPT-3 originality feedback, feedback during practice only, or no feedback; assignment to feedback conditions is not stated to be random (PDF pp. 8-11, 16). Study 2 randomly assigned museum visitors to immediate or delayed AuDrA feedback while completing drawings and reports an analyzed cleaned dataset of 36,198 people, without a separate people count after restricting models to the first two drawings per shape (PDF pp. 12-17). Both studies scored originality on human-produced outputs; Study 1 also assessed output produced after practice-only feedback was removed, and the feedback in both studies consisted only of numerical ratings (PDF pp. 9-14, 20, 31).

studies.label: Study 1: online design-problem experiment with numerical GPT-3 feedback

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants received continuous feedback, intermediate feedback during practice only, or no feedback. The document explicitly randomizes the sequence of design problems, but does not explicitly randomize people to the feedback conditions. Design class other preserves this uncertainty rather than asserting either randomized or non-random assignment.
assignment.quote: Condition was a between-participants factor with three levels (continuous feedback, intermediate feedback, no feedback).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 9), Procedure; PDF p. 12, Figure 2.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF pp. 2 and 15, Open access statement / Transparency and openness: https://aspredicted.org/bgmj-yrm4.pdf. PDF p. 15 lists the added intermediate condition, changed evaluation-accuracy analysis, and inclusion of engineers and non-engineers as deviations. The reconciler attempted the linked preregistration and the named OSF project's API with Python urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1; both failed with WinError 10013. No external document was obtained.

arms.name: Continuous feedback
arms.description: GPT-3 numerical originality feedback during practice and all scored design-problem trials; all groups also received repeated be-creative reminders. The pre-exclusion procedure reports 208 participants receiving this condition, but neither random assignment nor an unambiguous analyzed arm total is supplied (PDF p. 11; subgroup counts on p. 16). The generative_ai code identifies the GPT-3 model family; its numeric-only evaluative use remains a scope question.

arms.name: Intermediate feedback (practice only)
arms.description: GPT-3 numerical originality feedback during practice, with no feedback during scored trials. The procedure reports 214 participants receiving this condition before exclusions; random assignment and a reliable analyzed arm total are not stated (PDF p. 11; subgroup counts on p. 16).

arms.name: No feedback (control)
arms.description: No feedback during practice or scored trials; the same repeated be-creative reminders as the feedback groups. The procedure reports 208 participants before exclusions; random assignment and a reliable analyzed arm total are not stated (PDF p. 11; subgroup counts on p. 16).

participants.exclusions: Recruited: 629 adults (PDF p. 8). Invalid ideas, less than 1% of 8,173 initial entries, were removed after automated screening and human review; 11 participants were excluded for completion times more than three standard deviations from the average; 56 were identified with more than 25% of responses showing copy-and-paste behavior; 15 used a mobile phone/tablet; and 34 trials containing only one response were excluded (PDF pp. 15-16). The analyzed dataset is explicitly reported as 554 adults contributing 7,174 valid responses (p. 16). Overlap among participant exclusions is not stated. Arm totals remain null: the procedure counts conflict with the overall recruitment total, and p. 16 reports 327 engineers and 228 non-engineers whereas Table S1 reports 327 and 227 (PDF p. 43).
participants.who: English-speaking adults recruited through Prolific, including participants with and without engineering experience (PDF p. 8).
participants.country: United States, Canada, and United Kingdom (PDF p. 8).
participants.quote: The final dataset comprised 554 adults aged between 18 and 71 years
participants.locator: PDF p. 16 (printed p. 14), Data cleaning; recruitment on PDF p. 8; exclusions on pp. 15-16; Table S1 on p. 43.

ai_tool.how_used: Numerical evaluation of participants' own ideas, returned through an API after each submission. Scores were normalized to a 1-10 feedback scale and displayed graphically; the model provided no ideas or qualitative suggestions (PDF pp. 9-11, 31). The supplementary text identifies davinci-002 and a formatted problem/solution/rating completion used for fine-tuning (PDF p. 40). This is a generative language-model architecture used only as an originality scorer; whether such numerical feedback meets the atlas intervention scope is unresolved.

task.description: Generate creative solutions to improving clean-water access in remote areas, helping people with memory impairments remember tasks, and improving pedestrian-crossing safety. An unanalyzed practice problem asked for three solutions to improving remote learning. Up to 10 ideas were allowed for each scored problem (PDF pp. 8-9).
task.duration: 6 minutes per design problem (PDF p. 9); mean duration of the full study 33.62 minutes (PDF p. 11).

outcomes.name: Originality of design solutions with continuous feedback
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-3 originality scores on a 1-10 scale, recorded as ideas were submitted (PDF pp. 9-10, 20). The same scoring model supplied the feedback. Originality is analyzed per response, with participant and problem random intercepts, rather than as participant means (PDF pp. 16-18). The 7,174 observations are the common model dataset across all three arms, not the size of either pairwise contrast (PDF p. 16). Model 1 tests condition alone; Models 2 and 3 add response/trial order and self-ratings respectively and are variants of this same outcome (Table S3, PDF p. 45). Originality is tied to the paper's primary hypothesis on PDF p. 21. S1-O2 separates the practice-only contrast because scored production occurs after feedback removal.
outcomes.delay: Same session, with feedback continuing through the scored trials in the continuous-feedback arm (PDF p. 11).

contrasts.reported: Continuous feedback: EMM = 6.67, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [6.34, 7.00]; control: EMM = 6.13, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [5.79, 6.46]; t(8.50) = −3.56, p < .01; d = −0.35, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [−0.57, −0.13]. Table S3, condition (feedback): Model 1 b = 0.54 (SE = 0.15), p < .001; Model 2 b = 0.66 (SE = 0.20), p < .001; Model 3 b = 0.12 (SE = 0.24), p = .62. Negative d and t are preserved as printed; the feedback arm has the higher EMM. Model 3 adjusts for self-ratings and is a mechanism analysis, not a separate creativity outcome. The Discussion separately describes the benefit as d = 0.35 (PDF p. 29); this unsigned benefit description does not replace the signed result on p. 22.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22 (printed p. 20), Figure 3 caption and Does feedback drive changes in originality?; PDF p. 45 (printed supplementary p. 13), Table S3. PDF p. 29, Discussion, lines 587-590.

outcomes.name: Originality of unassisted design solutions after practice-only feedback
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same GPT-3 originality metric and common response-level mixed models as S1-O1, but the intermediate-feedback group receives no feedback while producing the scored solutions (PDF pp. 9-11, 16-18, 20). AI remains an unseen outcome scorer; this does not make AI assistance available to participants in the test phase. The 7,174 observations are shared across the full three-arm model, not the number of outputs in this two-arm contrast (PDF p. 16). Model variants are grouped here; Table S3 supplies the intermediate-versus-control coefficients (PDF p. 45). Originality is the outcome used to test the paper's primary hypothesis, including the three-arm condition model (PDF p. 21, lines 412-419; Table S3 on p. 45). The practice-only arm was added after preregistration (PDF p. 15), so paper_primary does not mean preregistered_primary. The ai_design contrast places this added practice-only configuration in treatment and continuous feedback in control; question = after_ai and ai_available_when_produced = no describe the practice-only treatment. The comparator retains feedback. The same comparison is not repeated under S1-O1.
outcomes.delay: Same session following practice; no elapsed interval is stated. Feedback is removed before the scored design-problem trials (PDF p. 11).

contrasts.reported: Intermediate feedback: EMM = 6.80, SE = 0.15, [6.46, 7.13]; control: EMM = 6.13, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [5.79, 6.46]; t(8.95) = −4.36, p < .01; d = −0.43, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [−0.66, −0.21]. Table S3, condition (intermediate): Model 1 b = 0.67 (SE = 0.15), p < .001; Model 2 b = 1.06 (SE = 0.21), p < .001; Model 3 b = 0.92 (SE = 0.24), p < .001. Negative d and t are preserved as printed; intermediate feedback has the higher EMM. The Discussion separately describes the practice-only benefit as d = 0.43 (PDF p. 29); the signed result on p. 22 is retained.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22 (printed p. 20), Does feedback drive changes in originality?; PDF p. 45 (printed supplementary p. 13), Table S3; feedback removal documented on PDF p. 11. PDF p. 29, Discussion, lines 587-590.

contrasts.reported: The continuous-versus-intermediate comparison is reported as d = 0.08, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.30]; t(3.80) = -0.86, p = .68. Intermediate EMM = 6.80, SE = 0.15; continuous EMM = 6.67, SE = 0.15. The paper's printed signs are retained without computing or reorienting an effect size. Practice-only feedback is the added configuration under test; continuous feedback is the reference configuration. Signs remain exactly as printed and are not recomputed.

studies.label: Study 2: museum drawing experiment with AuDrA feedback

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual museum visitors were assigned after a warm-up to immediate feedback after the first drawing or delayed feedback after two drawings. Subsequent drawings could receive feedback in both conditions; the primary analysis focuses on the first two drawings per shape (PDF pp. 14, 17).
assignment.quote: participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: immediate or delayed feedback.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 15, Transparency and openness, explicitly states that Study 2 was not preregistered. Table S9 is nonetheless headed (Preregistered analysis) on PDF p. 51; the explicit study-level statement is used here.

arms.name: Immediate feedback
arms.description: AuDrA numerical originality feedback after the first drawing, before production of the second. Coded other_aid because the identified AuDrA model is a convolutional neural network for scoring drawings, not an image generator. Assigned and analyzed counts are printed on PDF pp. 14 and 16.

arms.name: Delayed feedback (control for second drawing)
arms.description: AuDrA feedback begins after two drawings; the second drawing is produced before any feedback for that shape. Both conditions can receive feedback on later drawings. This is a no-feedback comparator during the primary scored phase, within a delayed-feedback arm (PDF pp. 14, 17, 47).

participants.exclusions: The initial total is 37,823 visitors (PDF p. 12), with assignment counts reported on p. 14. Drawings in the bottom 3% of completion times were excluded: 2,632 entries submitted in 6 seconds or less (PDF p. 16). The paper reports an analyzed cleaned dataset of 36,198 people and 77,142 drawings, with 18,136 people analyzed in immediate feedback and 18,062 in delayed feedback (p. 16). The number of people removed specifically by each exclusion is not stated. Analysis was restricted to the first two drawings per shape (p. 17); the number of people contributing a second drawing and the exact resulting model observation count are not separately reported.
participants.who: Science-museum visitors, including children with parent/guardian consent, participating in a Living Lab exhibit (PDF pp. 12-14).
participants.country: Poland (museum location; participant nationality not stated), PDF pp. 12-14.
participants.locator: PDF p. 16 (printed p. 14), Data cleaning; initial total on p. 12; random assignment and arm allocation counts on p. 14; analysis restriction on p. 17.

ai_tool.how_used: Predicts originality of submitted drawings and displays numerical feedback beside participants' own ratings (PDF p. 13). The Discussion explicitly identifies the model as a previously trained convolutional neural network (PDF p. 29). Although p. 13 also calls the scorer a fine-tuned large language model, the named system and the Discussion identify AuDrA, not a generative drawing tool. Feedback is numerical only (PDF p. 31); no generated image, idea, or qualitative suggestion is supplied.

task.description: Complete simple unfinished shapes to create something new and interesting on a touchscreen, using six possible shapes after a distinct warm-up task. Participants could make repeated drawings and choose further shapes; the main comparison uses the first two drawings per shape (PDF pp. 12-14, 17).
task.duration: No time constraints for individual drawings (PDF p. 13). Recruitment took place from June 2023 to June 2024 (PDF pp. 12-13).

outcomes.name: Drawing originality, principally the second drawing after immediate versus delayed feedback
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: AuDrA originality score, reported as ranging from 0 to 10 (PDF p. 20). The main contrast is the second drawing: the immediate group has received feedback, while the delayed group has not; the first drawing is baseline and later drawings in both groups may receive feedback (PDF p. 17). The feedback system remains in use, so this is not an after_ai withdrawal outcome. The pooled first/second-drawing analysis and models adding response/trial order or self-ratings are variants of the same metric (PDF pp. 23-24; Table S6, p. 48). Analysis uses output-level scores with participant and shape random intercepts (PDF pp. 16-18). The paper reports 77,142 drawings in the cleaned dataset but does not separately state the observation count for the first-two-per-shape restriction or the second-drawing contrast, so n_units is null. This answers the feedback-with-AI question descriptively, but AuDrA does not establish a generative-AI intervention. AI availability is coded mixed for the complete outcome record because it retains the unassisted first-drawing baseline, assisted second drawings in the immediate arm, and the pooled first/second model. For the focal second-drawing contrast alone, availability in the immediate-feedback arm is yes (PDF p. 17, lines 321-324; Table S5 note on p. 47).
outcomes.delay: Same session; immediate-arm participants see feedback on their first drawing before making the second (PDF pp. 14, 17). The word delayed in the control-arm name does not denote a later outcome session.

contrasts.reported: Primary second-drawing contrast: immediate feedback EMM = 4.84, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.79, 4.90]; delayed-feedback control EMM = 4.44, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.40, 4.48]; t(54,419) = −11.83, p < .001; d = −0.20, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [−0.24, −0.17] (PDF p. 24). Baseline first drawing: feedback EMM = 4.63, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.60, 4.67]; control EMM = 4.62, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.59, 4.66]; t(46,652) = −0.50, p = .62 (p. 24). The analysis including both first and second drawings reports feedback EMM = 4.65, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.62, 4.68], versus control EMM = 4.49, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [4.46, 4.52]; t(29,398) = −7.25, p < .001; d = −0.08, SE = 0.01, 95% CI [−0.10, −0.06] (p. 23). Table S6: Model 1 condition b = 0.16 (SE = 0.02), p < .001; Model 2 Response order × Condition b = 0.41 (SE = 0.03), p < .001 (p. 48). Negative d and t values are reproduced as printed, while the immediate-feedback condition has the higher post-feedback EMM. ai_vs_bau describes the absence of feedback in the control arm before its second drawing; the randomized arms differ in feedback timing. The Discussion describes the second-drawing benefit as d = 0.20 (PDF p. 29); the signed result on p. 24 is retained.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 22, Figure 3 caption; PDF pp. 23-24 (printed pp. 21-22), Does feedback drive changes in originality?; PDF p. 48 (printed supplementary p. 16), Table S6; phase-specific control definition on PDF pp. 17 and 47 (Table S5 notes). PDF p. 29, Discussion, lines 587-590.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Not stated for either intervention sample. The existing Study 1 corpus trains the scorer, and Study 2 uses a previously trained AuDrA model and validates it on drawings from the present study. These facts do not establish overlap of intervention participants with another paper.
sample_overlap.quote: The model was trained specifically for this study using an existing sample of design ideas
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 9, Development of AI feedback, lines 156-158; p. 29, Discussion, lines 600-603; p. 40, Supporting text.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is reported. Listed affiliations are universities and a science centre, funding is from public research agencies, and the authors declare no conflicts of interest. Use of GPT-3 is reported as a study tool, without a stated company role.
company_involvement.locator: PDF pp. 1-2, affiliations and Author Note; GPT-3 use on PDF p. 9.

eligibility.reason: Study 1 independently meets the size and output criteria: 554 adults were analyzed, and GPT-3 scored the originality of their own design solutions (PDF pp. 9, 16, 20-22; Table S1 on p. 43). Its feedback condition is between participants, but the stated random sequence concerns design problems, not allocation to feedback conditions or within-person AI-condition order (p. 11, Procedure; Figure 2 on p. 12). The complete manuscript and included supplement do not establish random feedback assignment; finalizer requests to the linked preregistration and OSF project API both failed with WinError 10013. Even accepting numerical feedback from fine-tuned GPT-3 davinci-002 as generative-AI assistance, criterion 1 therefore remains unclear. The existing scope question about numerical-only evaluative use is retained as a codebook-interpretation issue, not an unknown model identity or feedback format (pp. 9-10, 31, 40; creativity-codebook.md sections 1 and 3). Study 2 explicitly randomizes feedback timing and reports 36,198 analyzed people with output-scored drawing originality (pp. 13-17, 24), but its AuDrA convolutional network is a non-generative scoring aid (pp. 6, 29). Thus Study 2 does not meet the generative-AI component of criterion 1, despite random allocation, and cannot establish core eligibility. No study is confirmed to meet all three criteria. Unstated allocation in Study 1 does not establish non-random assignment, so its design class remains other and no observational context class is asserted.

one_line_finding: Feedback groups had higher model-scored originality: Study 1 EMM 6.67 with continuous feedback and 6.80 with practice-only feedback versus 6.13 in control (PDF p. 22), and Study 2 second-drawing EMM 4.84 with immediate versus 4.44 with delayed feedback (PDF p. 24).
open_questions: Was Study 1 feedback condition randomly assigned, including the added intermediate arm? PDF p. 11 states only random problem order, and Figure 2 on p. 12 does not specify allocation. The finalizer independently reviewed the full paper and supplement and retried the linked AsPredicted preregistration and OSF project API with Python urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1; both failed with WinError 10013. Random assignment to feedback remains unconfirmed.

Does the atlas include GPT-3 used solely to generate numerical originality ratings? The model and its score-completion format are documented on PDF pp. 9 and 40, while p. 31 states that feedback consisted of ratings only. AuDrA in Study 2 is a convolutional scoring network (pp. 6, 29); its explicit identification supersedes the inconsistent large-language-model wording on p. 13 for model coding. The remaining GPT-3 scope issue concerns applying creativity-codebook.md sections 1 and 3 to evaluative-only use, rather than obtaining an unreported empirical fact.

What are the correct Study 1 allocation and analyzed arm totals? Recruitment is 629 (PDF p. 8), while procedure counts are 208 continuous, 214 intermediate, and 208 control (p. 11). The final total is explicitly 554 (p. 16), but p. 16 reports 327 engineers and 228 non-engineers versus 327 and 227 in Table S1 (p. 43). Arm subgroup counts on p. 16 are 114/106/107 engineers and 76/75/77 non-engineers for continuous/intermediate/control. Randomized and analyzed arm totals remain null.

How many people and drawings contribute after Study 2 is restricted to the first two drawings per shape, and specifically to the second-drawing comparison? The paper reports an analyzed cleaned dataset of 36,198 people and 77,142 drawings (PDF p. 16); p. 17 gives the later restriction without separate retained counts. The reported cleaned participant total is retained and outcome n_units remains null.

Which measurement-development rater counts are correct? Study 1 reports 20 expert raters on PDF pp. 9 and 40 versus 40 on p. 29. Study 2 reports 141 validation raters on pp. 13 and 40 versus 120 on p. 29. These are not added to intervention participant counts.

What standardizer and precision conventions produced the reported d values and intervals? The PDF does not specify a recoverable standardizer for d (pp. 18, 22-24). It prints negative t and d despite higher feedback-arm means, and positive benefit magnitudes in the Discussion (p. 29). Study 2 EMM SE/CI combinations on pp. 23-24 and the control-intercept SE of 0.16 in Table S6 (p. 48), versus the control EMM SE of 0.02 on p. 23, require the original analysis output to explain; they need not represent the same estimand. No denominator, SE, interval, or sign has been inferred or corrected.

This supports paper_primary but not preregistered_primary for its originality outcome. S1-O1 and S1-O2 separate the same originality measure by assistance timing; their common 7,174-response model dataset must not be counted twice. Self-ratings, metacognitive evaluation accuracy, and mediation mechanisms are not additional externally scored creativity/diversity outcomes (pp. 18-19, 24-28; Tables S2, S4-S5, S7-S9). The paper reports no fluency, flexibility, usefulness, elaboration, convergent-test or across-person diversity treatment outcome. Its homogenization discussion cites other papers (p. 31). Human ratings used for scorer training and validation are measurement development, not additional assistance studies or intervention participants. Study 2 contrast-specific counts are not available. The summary total of 36,752 is the arithmetic sum of the two reported analyzed samples, 554 + 36,198, not a separately printed or deduplicated participant count. open_items.item: Study 1 feedback allocation (open_questions[0]): criterion 1 remains unclear. Author confirmation of the allocation method actually implemented for all three feedback arms, including the added intermediate arm, would settle it. An implemented survey randomizer or allocation record could also provide evidence; the linked preregistration and OSF API were inaccessible. Random task order is insufficient (PDF pp. 11-12, 15).

Numerical-only GPT-3 feedback scope (open_questions[1]): affects the generative-AI component of criterion 1. The paper already specifies the generative model, score-completion format, and ratings-only intervention (PDF pp. 9, 31, 40). An atlas interpretation of creativity-codebook.md sections 1 and 3 would settle this policy boundary; no further paper, supplement, data, or author evidence is needed. Study 1 allocation would remain unclear even if this use were included.

Study 1 inconsistent recruitment/allocation counts and analyzed arm totals (open_questions[2]): author correction of the conflicting counts would settle the arm sizes. This does not change the size criterion: the analyzed total is explicitly 554 (PDF p. 16), supported by Table S1 on p. 43. Keep randomized and analyzed arm counts null; do not sum inconsistent subgroup cells (recruitment on p. 8; allocation counts on p. 11).

Study 2 people and drawing counts after the first-two-per-shape restriction and for the second-drawing contrast (open_questions[3]): posted participant identifiers, drawing order, and analysis scripts would settle retained counts (PDF pp. 16-17). These are needed for extraction, but do not determine this paper's eligibility: Study 1 independently exceeds 50 analyzed people, and Study 2 fails the generative-AI requirement regardless of its restricted sample size. Keep the unreported outcome observation count null.

Conflicting scorer-training and validation rater counts (open_questions[4]): author clarification would settle the different counts on PDF pp. 9, 13, 29, and 40. These raters are measurement-development samples, not participants assigned to the creativity interventions, and therefore do not affect the eligibility people threshold or the existence of output-scored originality.

Effect-size standardizer and precision conventions (open_questions[5] and the unresolved reconciliation.differences entry open_questions.effect_size_standardizer_and_precision): posted analysis code and original model/post-hoc output would settle d's denominator, contrast orientation, and the SE/CI statements, including the distinction between the Table S6 intercept and marginal means (PDF pp. 18, 22-24, 29, 48). This affects effect-size extraction and pooling, not any of the three eligibility criteria. Retain all statistics as printed.
